1. Core Clinical Tension: A 37-year-old traveler returning to a non-endemic country (Japan) from West Africa (Nigeria) presents with progressive fever, headache, altered mental status, jaundice, severe thrombocytopenia (17,000/µL), and markedly elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 23.14 mg/dL). Despite typical symptoms, he was twice misdiagnosed in the outpatient setting with a common cold. The central diagnostic challenge is differentiating common respiratory/viral illness or severe pyogenic sepsis from acute cerebral malaria with multi-organ involvement following delayed diagnosis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission clinical presentation concludes with emergency triage vital signs (fever 38.5 °C, tachycardia 126 bpm, tachypnea 28 breaths/min), altered mental status (GCS 14), conjunctival icterus, and initial triage laboratory findings (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, platelets 17,000/µL, total bilirubin 5.1 mg/dL, CRP 23.14 mg/dL), immediately before the examination of the peripheral blood smear, rapid antigen test, and confirmatory PCR.
3. Differential Distinctions: Viral upper respiratory infection ('common cold') is the most frequent outpatient misdiagnosis for acute tropical fevers but is completely inconsistent with profound thrombocytopenia, marked hyperbilirubinemia, and altered sensorium; acute bacterial sepsis with DIC causes high fever, tachycardia, elevated CRP, and thrombocytopenia, but the patient failed oral cephalosporin therapy (cefaclor) and lacked localized pyogenic foci; whereas severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria uniquely accounts for hyperparasitemia-induced hemolysis, severe consumptive thrombocytopenia, acute hyperbilirubinemia, and impaired consciousness (cerebral malaria).
case_prompt:
A 37-year-old male was transferred by emergency ambulance to a tertiary hospital due to high fever, progressive fatigue, and acute cognitive alteration. The patient had returned to Japan two weeks prior following a six-month business trip to Nigeria. He had not taken any travel chemoprophylaxis, had not utilized insect repellent, and recalled sustaining frequent mosquito bites during his stay.

Six days prior to admission, he developed generalized malaise, high fever, and severe headache. Five days before admission, he was evaluated at a local outpatient clinic, where he was diagnosed with an acute common cold and prescribed oral loxoprofen and cefaclor. Three days before admission, he sought care at a second outpatient clinic for persistent fevers and worsening malaise; he was again diagnosed with an uncomplicated common cold. Over the subsequent 48 hours, his symptoms failed to improve, and he became confused, lethargic, and disoriented, prompting his family to call emergency services.

On arrival at the emergency department, his mental status examination revealed impaired consciousness with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14 (E4V4M6). Vital signs included a blood pressure of 138/87 mmHg, heart rate of 126 beats/min, body temperature of 38.5 °C, respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation of 98% while breathing ambient air. Physical examination revealed conjunctival and scleral icterus. No rash or focal neurological deficits were noted.

Immediate triage laboratory testing demonstrated a hemoglobin level of 12.5 g/dL, severe thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 17,000/µL, marked hyperbilirubinemia with a total bilirubin level of 5.1 mg/dL, and a markedly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 23.14 mg/dL.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Viral upper respiratory tract infection ('common cold')
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Repeatedly diagnosed in outpatient clinics; however, an uncomplicated upper respiratory tract viral illness does not account for altered consciousness, severe thrombocytopenia (17,000/µL), and marked hyperbilirubinemia (5.1 mg/dL).
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Five days prior to admission, he visited a clinic nearby and was diagnosed with common cold. Loxoprofen and cefaclor were prescribed. Three days prior to admission, he visited another clinic and was again diagnosed with common cold. His symptoms had not improved, and his mental state appeared altered.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Severe bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to high fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, severe thrombocytopenia, and elevated CRP (23.14 mg/dL), but the patient had deteriorated despite oral cephalosporin therapy (cefaclor) and showed prominent hemolysis without septic shock.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Loxoprofen and cefaclor were prescribed... His symptoms had not improved... thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 17 000 /muL, high bilirubinemia with a total bilirubin level of 5.1 mg/dL, and elevated inflammatory markers, with elevated C-reactive protein levels of 23.14 mg/dL.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Emergency microscopic examination of the peripheral blood smear revealed erythrocytes parasitized by Plasmodium falciparum ring forms with a parasitemia index of 5.4%, confirmed by a positive rapid immunochromatographic antigen test and PCR.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The examination of his peripheral blood smear showed P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes with a parasitemia index of 5.4% (Figure 1). A rapid immunographic test (Binax NOW Malaria Test; Binax, Portland, OR) result for P. falciparum was positive.

editor_comments: Case distilled with strict adherence to admission breakpoint. Peripheral blood smear, rapid diagnostic test, PCR, and antimalarial treatments excluded from case prompt.
